lines.text: Patterns and textures add visual interest and tactile quality to fabrics, surfaces, and designs. A pattern is a repeated decorative design — stripes run in parallel lines (horizontal, vertical, or diagonal), while checks and plaids are grids of intersecting lines in multiple colours. Polka dots are circles of uniform size arranged evenly, and floral patterns feature flowers and botanical motifs. Geometric patterns use shapes — triangles, hexagons, and diamonds — arranged in repeating formations. Paisley features curved, teardrop-shaped motifs originating from Persian design. Camouflage uses irregular shapes in earthy tones for concealment. Abstract patterns are non-representational and artistic. Texture describes how a surface feels or appears to feel. Smooth surfaces — silk, glass, polished marble — have no roughness. Rough textures — sandpaper, tree bark, raw stone — have an uneven, coarse surface. Soft textures include velvet, fleece, and cotton; hard textures include metal, wood, and ceramic. Other textural words include glossy (shiny), matte (non-reflective), bumpy, grainy, fuzzy, silky, coarse, and fine. In fashion, describing both pattern and texture is essential: 'a soft, striped cashmere scarf' or 'a glossy, floral silk blouse' convey both visual and tactile qualities.

lines.text: Tartan is the specific crossed-line pattern associated with Scottish clans — each clan has its own registered tartan. 'Plaid' is the general American English term for any checked fabric. In British English, 'plaid' can specifically mean a tartan cloth worn as a shawl.

lines.text: The paisley pattern originated in Persia and was named after the Scottish town of Paisley, which mass-produced paisley shawls in the 19th century. Today, paisley is associated with bohemian fashion and vintage style in English-speaking cultures.

lines.text: English uses texture words for food too: 'crispy' (chips), 'crunchy' (cereal), 'creamy' (soup), 'chewy' (toffee), 'flaky' (pastry), 'tender' (meat), 'juicy' (fruit). Food texture vocabulary overlaps significantly with fabric and material descriptions.

lines.text: Classic English fabric patterns include 'herringbone' (V-shaped weave, like fish bones), 'houndstooth' (jagged check pattern), and 'pinstripe' (very thin stripes). These are traditional patterns in British tailoring and professional menswear.

lines.text: In English fashion vocabulary, 'pattern mixing' (wearing different patterns together) is a recognized style technique. Rules include mixing scales (large + small patterns) and keeping a consistent colour palette. 'Clashing patterns' means patterns that don't work together.
